idiom_name: queue.Queue(maxsize=n) - put/put_nowait/timeout; asyncio.Queue(maxsize=n) for the async twin
implementation_notes: The standard library ships the pattern with the policy selected by the call: Queue(maxsize=n) blocks in put() until a slot frees, raises queue.Full from put_nowait()/put(block=False), and bounds the wait with put(item, timeout=t); since 3.13 a queue can also be shut down, after which producers get queue.ShutDown instead of blocking forever. The asyncio twin asyncio.Queue(maxsize=n) has the same contract with await put()/put_nowait() and asyncio.QueueFull, so the design decision is made once per concurrency model rather than once per project. A hand-written buffer is only justified for policies the stdlib lacks (drop-oldest, coalescing) or for per-item attribution.
pitfalls: put() on a full queue blocks forever unless a consumer runs: default-constructed blocking puts are the most common way this pattern deadlocks a thread pool.
The unfinished-task counter is not the bound: if you evict items yourself (get_nowait) to make room, join() never returns because their task_done() was never called.
maxsize=0 (or negative) means infinite, which is the default constructor argument - the bound disappears unless it is stated explicitly.

variants.name: collections.deque with maxlen (drop-oldest)
variants.implementation_notes: Where losing the oldest item is the right policy, the standard library provides the bound as a data-structure property: a deque with maxlen never exceeds that length and, once full, discards items from the opposite end, so a rolling window needs no locks, no exceptions and no capacity checks. append/popleft are O(1) and individually atomic under the GIL, which makes deque(maxlen=n) the natural bounded buffer for metrics, logs, last-N state and any consumer that can tolerate a sliding window. The classic queue structure is still the right tool when producers must block or be refused, when the loss must be attributed, or when several threads act on the window as a whole.
variants.idiom_name: collections.deque(maxlen=n) - evicts from the opposite end when full
pitfalls: Eviction is silent and unconditional: there is no reject or block option, so the drop policy exists whether or not you count it.
Atomic per operation does not mean compound operations are safe: len(d) == d.maxlen followed by append double-counts across threads under the GIL.
Iterating a deque while another thread appends raises RuntimeError (mutated during iteration); snapshot under a lock before iterating.
